question: What is the medical term for infective bone disease?

options.A: Osteoarthritis
options.B: Osteoporosis
options.C: Osteomyelitis
options.D: Osteomalacia

explanation: Osteomyelitis is the specific term used to describe an infection and inflammation of the bone and bone marrow. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why does infection inside a bone cause tissue death much faster than infections in soft tissue?

options.A: Bone is trapped inside a rigid structure where swelling cuts off its blood supply
options.B: The periosteum actively feeds the bacteria instead of protecting the bone
options.C: Bones lack white blood cells entirely to fight off invading bacteria
options.D: Microorganisms multiply twice as fast inside hard calcium deposits

explanation: Because bone cannot expand, swelling and pus create high pressure inside the rigid bone cavity, which compresses blood vessels and starves the tissue of oxygen. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h1)

question: Which bacterium is responsible for the majority of bone infection cases?

options.A: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.B: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.C: Staphylococcus aureus
options.D: Escherichia coli

explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the leading pathogen isolated in almost all forms of osteomyelitis, whether acute or chronic. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h2)

question: A patient develops a bone infection in the foot after stepping on a nail while wearing sneakers. Which organism is most likely involved?

options.A: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.B: Salmonella typhi
options.C: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
options.D: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

explanation: Puncture wounds through rubber-soled shoes, like trainers, commonly introduce Pseudomonas bacteria directly into the foot bones. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h2)

question: What is the term for a piece of dead bone separated from living bone during osteomyelitis?

options.A: Cortex
options.B: Involucrum
options.C: Callus
options.D: Sequestrum

explanation: A sequestrum is the segment of necrotic bone that has lost its blood supply due to severe infection and pressure. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h3)

question: What role does the involucrum play in chronic bone infection?

options.A: It is the primary channel through which bacteria enter the bloodstream
options.B: It is a soft tissue tumor that mimics bone cancer on an X-ray
options.C: It acts as a sponge that absorbs antibiotics and neutralizes them
options.D: It is new bone formed by the periosteum to wall off the dead bone

explanation: The body creates an outer shell of living new bone called an involucrum around the dead bone segment during the chronic phase. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common risk factor for developing osteomyelitis?

options.A: Recent bone surgery
options.B: Diabetes mellitus
options.C: Intravenous drug use
options.D: Regular aerobic exercise

explanation: Regular physical activity strengthens the body and is not a risk factor for bone infections, unlike diabetes, drug use, and surgery. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h4)

question: How does hematogenous osteomyelitis differ from contiguous osteomyelitis?

options.A: Hematogenous spreads through the blood from another body site, while contiguous enters from direct contact with an outside source
options.B: Hematogenous is caused exclusively by viruses, while contiguous is bacterial
options.C: Hematogenous heals on its own without drugs, while contiguous requires amputation
options.D: Hematogenous only affects children, while contiguous only affects elderly patients

explanation: Hematogenous osteomyelitis travels via the bloodstream from a distant infection, whereas contiguous osteomyelitis spreads from a nearby wound, ulcer, or surgery. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h4)

question: What is a key characteristic of bone pain caused by osteomyelitis?

options.A: It completely disappears when the patient rests in bed
options.B: It shifts to a different bone every few hours
options.C: It is a constant, throbbing pain that worsens with movement
options.D: It only occurs when the patient eats cold foods

explanation: Bone pain from infection is typically deep, constant, throbbing, and intensified by physical activity or pressure on the site. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h5)

question: A nurse assesses an adult patient with suspected acute osteomyelitis. Which set of findings is most expected?

options.A: Yellowing of the eyes, dark urine, and severe abdominal cramping
options.B: High fever, localized bone pain, swelling, and extreme tenderness
options.C: Numbness in both hands, low blood pressure, and a dry cough
options.D: Painless joint stiffness, dry skin, and generalized hair loss

explanation: Acute osteomyelitis classically triggers both systemic signs of infection like fever and distinct local signs like pain, warmth, and swelling at the bone site. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h5)

question: Why might a standard X-ray appear completely normal during the very first week of acute osteomyelitis?

options.A: X-rays cannot pass through calcium deposits in the human skeleton
options.B: Early bacterial infections only attack the blood and never the bone tissue
options.C: Significant bone destruction must occur before it becomes visible on an X-ray
options.D: Radiation from the X-ray machine temporarily hides early bone changes

explanation: Standard X-rays require about 30 to 50 percent bone matrix loss before changes show up, meaning early infection is often missed on plain films. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h6)

question: Which diagnostic imaging tool is best for detecting early bone marrow inflammation and infection?

options.A: Abdominal ultrasound
options.B: Standard chest radiograph
options.C: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.D: Electrocardiogram

explanation: MRI provides excellent soft tissue and bone marrow detail, making it the most sensitive imaging method for early-stage osteomyelitis. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h6)

question: What is the typical duration of antibiotic therapy for osteomyelitis?

options.A: 3 to 5 days
options.B: 24 to 48 hours
options.C: 4 to 6 weeks or longer
options.D: Exactly one year

explanation: Because antibiotics penetrate bone tissue slowly, treatment requires a prolonged course, usually lasting several weeks to clear the infection fully. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h7)

question: Why is long-term intravenous therapy often administered via a PICC line for osteomyelitis patients?

options.A: It forces the antibiotic medication to bypass the stomach and land directly inside the infected bone cavity
options.B: It allows safe, long-term delivery of strong antibiotics directly into the bloodstream without frequent needle sticks
options.C: It prevents the patient from experiencing any side effects from the medication
options.D: It increases the white blood cell count within minutes of insertion

explanation: A PICC line provides reliable venous access for weeks of home or outpatient IV antibiotic therapy, sparing peripheral veins from damage. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of surgical debridement in osteomyelitis?

options.A: To permanently fuse the adjacent joint together
options.B: To increase skin pigmentation over the surgical site
options.C: To remove infected, necrotic bone and debris
options.D: To replace the entire skeleton with artificial metal rods

explanation: Debridement physically cleans out dead bone and pus that antibiotics cannot easily reach, giving healthy tissue a chance to heal. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h8)

question: Why do surgeons sometimes place antibiotic-impregnated beads into a bone cavity after debridement?

options.A: To act as a permanent anchor for future muscle attachments
options.B: To deliver a high concentration of medication directly to the infection site
options.C: To attract white blood cells away from the rest of the body
options.D: To permanently replace missing calcium and strengthen the bone

explanation: Antibiotic beads release local medication directly into the wound bed at high levels without causing systemic toxicity. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h8)

question: A patient scheduled for discharge on home IV antibiotics says they want to stop the medicine early because the pain is gone. How should the nurse respond?

options.A: Suggest waiting until the next scheduled clinic visit in three months
options.B: Tell the patient to double their pill dose to make up for the missed days
options.C: Explain that stopping early can cause the infection to return stronger and harder to treat
options.D: Agree and instruct the patient to take over-the-counter pain pills instead

explanation: Patients must finish their entire course of antibiotics to ensure all bacteria are eradicated, preventing a relapse of chronic osteomyelitis. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h9)

question: Which dietary recommendation is most important for a patient recovering from a severe bone infection?

options.A: Low calorie intake to prevent any weight gain during bed rest
options.B: Strictly liquid diet to rest the digestive system after surgery
options.C: High sodium diet to maintain normal blood pressure levels
options.D: High protein and vitamin C intake to promote tissue and bone healing

explanation: Healing bone requires adequate nutrition, particularly proteins and vitamins, to rebuild damaged cellular matrix and fight infection. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h9)

question: Which of the following is a frequent long-term complication of poorly treated acute osteomyelitis?

options.A: Rheumatoid arthritis
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
options.D: Chronic osteomyelitis

explanation: When acute bone infections are not fully eradicated, they frequently transition into long-standing chronic osteomyelitis with recurrent flare-ups. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h10)

question: Why is bone weakened enough to cause a pathological fracture in a patient with chronic osteomyelitis?

options.A: The infection turns all the solid bone into liquid fat deposits
options.B: Antibiotic medications dissolve the calcium inside the bone matrix
options.C: Muscles pull so hard on the bone that they snap it in half
options.D: Extensive areas of bone death and destruction compromise the structural integrity

explanation: Areas of necrotic bone and chronic destruction weaken the overall structural framework of the bone, making it prone to breaking under normal stress. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h10)
